TIGHT APPROXIMATION FOR RATIONALLY SIMPLY
CONNECTED VARIETIES
OLIVIER BENOIST AND OLIVIER WITTENBERG
Abstract. We prove that holomorphic maps from an open subset of a complex smooth projective curve to a complex smooth projective rationally simply
connected variety can be approximated by algebraic maps for the compact-open
topology. This theorem can be applied in particular when the target is a smooth
hypersurface of degree d in Pn
C with n ≥d2 −1. We deduce it from a more general
result: the tight approximation property holds for rationally simply connected
varieties over function ﬁelds of complex curves.
1. Introduction
Algebraic approximation problems for holomorphic maps are central in complex
algebraic geometry. We will focus on the following precise question.
Question 1.1. Let B and X be smooth projective algebraic varieties over C. Suppose
that B is a connected curve. Let Ω⊂B(C) be an open subset. Can all holomorphic
maps Ω→X(C) be approximated by algebraic maps (that is, by maps induced by
morphisms of algebraic varieties B →X) for the compact-open topology?
The archetype of such a result is Runge’s theorem and its generalizations by
Behnke–Stein [BS49] and Royden [Roy67], which yield a positive answer to Question 1.1 for X = P1
C (see [Roy67, Theorem 10]).
Further positive answers were
obtained when X is a Grassmannian (see [Kuc95, Theorem 1]) and when X is a
rational surface [BK03, Corollary 1.2]. More generally, a positive answer was given
to Question 1.1 when X is birational to an iterated ﬁbration into homogeneous spaces
under connected linear algebraic groups (combine [BW21, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 5.1
and Theorem 7.4]). This class of varieties includes smooth cubic hypersurfaces of
dimension ≥2 and smooth complete intersections of two quadrics of dimension ≥2
(see [BW21, Examples 5.4 and 5.6]).
In addition, Forstnerič and Lárusson have
answered Question 1.1 positively when X is birational to an algebraically elliptic
smooth projective variety (see [FL25, Corollary 1.8]); in view of [KZ24, Corollary 1.4],
this recovers the case of smooth cubic hypersurfaces of dimension ≥2.

The answer to Question 1.1 can also be in the negative, for instance when B = P1
C
and X is an elliptic curve; more generally, a positive answer implies that b1(X) = 0
(see [BK03, Corollary 1.3]). We do not know the answer for any K3 surface X.
It was suggested in [BW21, Question 3.6] that Question 1.1 should have a positive
answer whenever X is rationally connected, i.e. whenever any two general points
of X(C) can be joined by a rational curve. In this article, we provide an answer for
rationally simply connected varieties.
Theorem 1.2. Question 1.1 has a positive answer whenever X is rationally simply
connected.
The class of rationally simply connected varieties is more restricted than the class of
rationally connected varieties: one not only requires that X be rationally connected,
but also that some spaces of rational curves on X themselves be rationally connected.
These varieties were ﬁrst introduced by Starr [Sta06]; their theory was developed by
de Jong and Starr [dJS06] and in the far-reaching work of de Jong, He and Starr
[dJHS11]. Various deﬁnitions have appeared in the literature. We refer to §2.1 for
the one that we use in this article and that is close to Hassett’s [Has10, Theorem 4.7].
The main concrete applications of Theorem 1.2 come from the fact that smooth
complete intersections of suﬃciently low degree in weighted projective spaces are
known to be rationally simply connected, by the works of de Jong and Starr [dJS06]
and Minoccheri [Min20]. In §2.2, we recall their results and verify their compatibility
with the deﬁnition of rationally simply connected variety that we use. In the case of
hypersurfaces in projective space, we deduce the following corollary.
Corollary 1.3. Question 1.1 has a positive answer for smooth hypersurfaces of
degree d in Pn
C whenever n ≥d2 −1.
This was previously only known when n ≥φ(d) for some function φ : N →N
with superexponential growth (see [BW21, Example 5.5]).
It has been understood since [BK03] that it is better to consider a reinforcement
of Question 1.1 allowing for jet conditions at ﬁnitely many points of Ω. (Such jet
conditions are taken into account in [BW21] and [FL25].) In addition, in [BW21],
we proposed studying Question 1.1 for one-parameter families of algebraic varieties
rather than for a ﬁxed algebraic variety. Our setup is the following.
Let B be a connected smooth projective curve over C.
Let X be a smooth
projective variety over C(B) and let f : X →B be a projective regular model
of X. We say that X satisﬁes the tight approximation property if any holomorphic
section u of f over an open subset Ω⊂B(C) can be approximated, for the compactopen topology, by algebraic sections that have the same jets as u at ﬁnitely many

Theorem 3.1]). When X comes, by scalar extension, from a variety X0 deﬁned over C,

Any smooth, projective, rationally simply connected variety over C(B) satisﬁes the

of rational curves and in particular on the Graber–Harris–Starr theorem [GHS03]; in

Shiﬀman [DLS94, Theorem 1.1].
Here is a more precise outline of the proof of Theorem 1.4. Choose a projective
regular model f : X →B of X. Let u : Ω→X(C) be the holomorphic section of f
over Ω⊂B(C) to be approximated by algebraic maps. The Nash approximation
result [DLS94, Theorem 1.1] applied to u allows us to ensure that u(Ω) ⊂B′(C)

for some algebraic curve B′ ⊂X all of whose irreducible components dominate B.
Making use of the rational simple connectedness of X, we construct a comb Z ⊂X
whose Zariski closure in X contains B′ and hence u(Ω). The idea is then to deform Z
to a rational curve on X, to simultaneously deform u so that u(Ω) now belongs
to the Zariski closure in X of this rational curve, and to conclude by applying the
(known) tight approximation property for rational curves (Royden’s theorem [Roy67,
Theorem 10], or see [BW21, Theorem 4.2]). The hardest aspect of the proof (and
one that is absent from [Has10]) is the need to ensure, by means of careful choices
of X, B′ and Z, that the Zariski closures in X of the comb, as well as of its small
deformations, are smooth over B in a neighborhood of u(Ω). This key property is
what allows us to deform u with the comb.
The point of view of tight approximation is useful even if one only wants to prove
Theorem 1.4 for a rationally simply connected variety X over C(B) that comes, by
extension of scalars, from a variety X0 deﬁned over C. Indeed, in this case, the model
of X on which the proof takes place may not be the constant ﬁbration X0 × B →B.
Even though the article [BW21] also deﬁnes and studies the tight approximation
property in the more general context of real algebraic geometry, we are unable to
prove a real counterpart of Theorem 1.4 (or of its consequence Theorem 1.2), because
many of our arguments break down in this extended setting; for instance, the Graber–
Harris–Starr theorem plays a key role in the proof, but no real analogue of it is known.
Organization of the text. After recalling general facts concerning rationally
simply connected varieties in Section 2 and concerning the tight approximation
property in Section 3, we give the proof of Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.5 in Section 4.

We also thank

2. Reminders on rationally simply connected varieties
2.1. Deﬁnition of rationally simply connected varieties. Let k be a ﬁeld of
characteristic 0. An integral projective variety X over k is rationally connected if for
any algebraically closed ﬁeld extension k ⊂l, any two general points x, y ∈X(l) are
in the image of a rational curve P1
l →Xl (see [Kol96, IV, Deﬁnition 3.2.2]). Being
rationally connected is a birational invariant of integral projective varieties over k.
We will make use of Kontsevich’s moduli spaces of stable maps (see [FP97] for an

In the case when X is a smooth projective rationally connected variety over k, the
following result holds.
Theorem 2.1. Let k be a ﬁeld of characteristic 0. Let X be a smooth, projective,
rationally connected variety over k. Then, for any g, n ≥0, the moduli space Mg,n(X)
is irreducible of dimension (dim X + n(g −1) + 1). Moreover, the evaluation
morphism ev : Mg,n(X) →Xn is dominant.
This is a result of de Jong and Starr ([dJS06, Theorem 1.1]). In the case when
k = C, it is also proved by Kollár and by Starr ([dJHS11, Theorem 1.1]). The
dimension formula for Mg,n(X) is also due to Kollár [Kol96, IV, Theorem 3.2.3]
in the case when X is rationally connected over C, and by de Jong and
Starr [dJS06, Theorem 1.1] in general.

2.2. Rationally simply connected varieties. We refer to [dJS06, Deﬁnition
3.1] for the deﬁnition of rationally simply connected varieties. For the convenience
of the reader, we recall that an integral projective variety X over a ﬁeld k of
characteristic 0 is rationally simply connected if for any algebraically closed ﬁeld
extension k ⊂l, any two points x, y ∈X(l) are in the image of a rational curve
P1
l →Xl, and if for any x ∈X(l), the space of rational curves through x has
a component which is rationally connected and has Picard number 1.

A smooth projective variety X over C is rationally simply connected if the following
two conditions hold (see [dJS06, Theorem 3.6]):

(a) X is rationally connected (i.e. any two points can be connected by a
rational curve),

(b) any two points of X(C) can be connected by a family of rational curves whose
general member is smooth (i.e. the family of rational curves has smooth general
member).

In the case when X is a smooth complete intersection of low degree in a weighted
projective space, this is ensured by [dJS06, Theorem 3.9] and [dJS06, Theorem
3.10].

In addition, we have the following result, which is a consequence of [dJS06,
Theorem 3.13].

Proposition 2.2. Let k be a ﬁeld of characteristic 0. Let X be a smooth, projective,
rationally simply connected variety over k. Then, for any g, n ≥0, the moduli
space Mg,n(X) is irreducible of dimension (dim X + n(g −1) + 1). Moreover, the
evaluation morphism ev : Mg,n(X) →Xn is dominant.

This is also a result of de Jong and Starr. In the case when k = C, it is proved
in [dJHS11, Theorem 1.1] that the moduli spaces Mg,n(X) are irreducible and that
the evaluation morphism is dominant.

2.3. The deﬁnition of rationally simply connected is not entirely symmetric in
the two conditions. In the case of (a), we only require that X is rationally connected.
In the case of (b), we require that the space of rational curves through a general point
has a component with Picard number 1 and that the family of rational curves has
smooth general member. 

As a result, in the case of (a), the variety X may not be simply connected in
the topological sense, even if k = C. On the other hand, in the case of (b), we have
the following consequence.

Proposition 2.3. Let X be a smooth, projective, rationally simply connected variety
over C. Then, for any two points x, y ∈X(C), there exists a rational curve connecting
x and y, with a smooth member of the family of rational curves.

This is proved in [dJS06, Theorem 3.13].

2.4. The deﬁnition of rationally simply connected is also adapted to the case when
X is deﬁned over a non-closed ﬁeld. For instance, if X is a smooth, projective,
rationally simply connected variety over C(B), then for any closed point b ∈ B, the
specialization Xb is a smooth, projective, rationally simply connected variety over C.
